questions.question: Which of the following article of the Indian constitution promotes equal justice and free legal aid?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 39 A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 39A** of the **Indian Constitution** directs the state to ensure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid to economically weaker sections of society.
 
• This article was introduced by the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976** under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• It mandates the state to ensure that no citizen is denied access to justice due to economic or other disabilities.
 
• The provision emphasizes the importance of creating a fair and equitable judicial system accessible to all, irrespective of their financial status.
 
• The implementation of **free legal aid services** has been institutionalized through the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, which established **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** to oversee legal aid programs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are non-justiciable rights enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, aimed at guiding the state in governance and policy-making to establish a welfare state.
 
• These principles are inspired by the **Irish Constitution** and aim to promote social and economic justice.
 
• Though not enforceable in a court of law, they are fundamental in the governance of the country and are intended to be implemented by legislative and executive actions.
 
 
 
• **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987:**
 
 
• This act was enacted to provide free and competent legal services to weaker sections of society and to ensure justice for all.
 
• It led to the creation of institutions like **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** at the national level and **State Legal Services Authorities (SLSA)** at the state level.
 
• These institutions provide free legal aid, conduct Lok Adalats, and spread legal awareness.
 
 
 
• **Article 38:**
 
 
• Article 38 directs the state to strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting a social order based on justice, social, economic, and political.
 
• It focuses on minimizing inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities among individuals and groups.
 
 
 
• **Other Related Articles:**
 
 
• **Article 45:** Originally directed the state to provide free and compulsory education for children below the age of 14; later amended to focus on early childhood care and education for children below six years.
 
• **Article 42:** Directs the state to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of NALSA:**

 
 
• NALSA was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and works to provide free legal services to the weaker sections of society.
 
• It organizes **Lok Adalats** to resolve disputes through alternative dispute resolution mechanisms.
 
• NALSA also promotes legal awareness through campaigns and programs at the grassroots level.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Article 39A:**
 
 
• It is a cornerstone of India's commitment to ensuring justice for all.
 
• It reflects the constitutional vision of building an inclusive judicial system that does not discriminate against marginalized groups.
 
• Free legal aid under this article is a step toward achieving the goal of **social and economic justice**.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective:**
 
 
• Many countries have similar provisions to ensure access to justice, such as the **Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act, 2012** in the **UK**.
 
• The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)** also emphasizes the right to access justice without discrimination.

questions.question: Who among the Following was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2024?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Karpoori Thakur (Posthumous)**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Karpoori Thakur** was a prominent Indian politician and social reformer who served as the **Chief Minister of Bihar** for two terms (1970-1971 and 1977-1979). 
 
• He was an advocate of **social justice**, focusing on the upliftment of marginalized communities, particularly Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. 
 
• Known as the **Jan Nayak** (People's Leader), he implemented policies that promoted **reservations** for backward classes in educational institutions and government jobs. 
 
• Karpoori Thakur's contributions towards social equality and his relentless efforts for the welfare of oppressed sections of society earned him widespread respect and recognition. 
 
• In 2024, he was honored with the **Bharat Ratna posthumously**, India's highest civilian award, for his exemplary contributions to Indian politics and social reform. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Bharat Ratna:** 
 
 
• The **Bharat Ratna** is India's highest civilian award, instituted in **1954**. 
 
• It is awarded for exceptional service or performance of the highest order in any field of human endeavor. 
 
• The award is presented by the **President of India** and does not carry any monetary grant. 
 
• Recipients receive a **peepal leaf-shaped medallion** and a certificate signed by the President. 
 
 
 
• **Other Bharat Ratna recipients:** 
 
 
• **Lata Mangeshkar** (awarded in 2001, posthumously celebrated for her contributions to Indian music). 
 
• **Atal Bihari Vajpayee** (awarded in 2015, celebrated for his role as India's Prime Minister and contributions to Indian politics). 
 
• **Sachin Tendulkar** (awarded in 2014, recognized for his achievements in cricket). 
 
 
 
• **Karpoori Thakur's Legacy:** 
 
 
• He was the first leader to implement **reservation policies** for backward classes in Bihar. 
 
• Thakur emphasized the importance of **inclusive governance** and was known for his simplicity and integrity. 
 
• He played a significant role in promoting **social justice** and empowering underprivileged communities. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Posthumous Awards:** 
 
 
• Posthumous Bharat Ratna awards are given to individuals whose contributions continue to inspire generations even after their demise. 
 
• Some notable posthumous recipients include **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** (1990) and **M.G. Ramachandran** (1988). 
 
 
 
• **Selection Process:** 
 
 
• The Bharat Ratna is awarded based on recommendations made by the **Prime Minister** to the President. 
 
• No formal nominations are required, and the number of annual recipients is restricted to **three**.

questions.question: In the Union Budget 2025-26, the government has allocated Rs. 20000 crores for an initiative aiming to develop at least ______ indigenously designed and operational SMRs by 2033.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• The Union Budget 2025-26 allocated **Rs. 20,000 crores** for an initiative to develop **indigenously designed and operational Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)** by **2033**. 
 
• The goal is to develop at least **5 operational SMRs**, which is considered a feasible and ambitious target for the given timeline and budget allocation. 
 
• **SMRs (Small Modular Reactors)** are advanced nuclear reactors that offer high flexibility, enhanced safety, and lower capital investment compared to traditional nuclear reactors. 
 
• This initiative aligns with India’s goal to enhance **energy security** and reduce **carbon emissions** by adopting cleaner and sustainable energy solutions. 
 
• The development of SMRs will contribute to India’s **Make in India** initiative, promoting indigenous technologies and creating opportunities for skilled employment. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Small Modular Reactors (SMRs):** 
 
 
• **Definition:** SMRs are nuclear reactors that are smaller in size, typically producing **up to 300 MW** of electricity per reactor module. 
 
• **Features:** They are designed to be scalable, allowing multiple modules to be combined to meet energy demands. 
 
• **Advantages:** SMRs offer **enhanced safety** features, reduced costs, and shorter construction times compared to conventional nuclear reactors. 
 
• **Applications:** SMRs are ideal for **remote locations, industrial applications, and water desalination**. 
 
 
 
• **Global SMR Development:** 
 
 
• Countries such as **Canada, the US, Russia, and China** are actively investing in SMR technologies. 
 
• Canada’s **National SMR Action Plan** aims to deploy SMRs for clean energy and economic development. 
 
• The US Department of Energy (DOE) has provided funding for SMR development under the **Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program**. 
 
 
 
• **India’s Nuclear Energy Program:** 
 
 
• India currently operates several nuclear power plants and aims to increase its nuclear energy capacity to **22 GW** by 2031. 
 
• Organizations like the **Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)** and **Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL)** are key players in nuclear energy development. 
 
 
 
• **Make in India Initiative:** 
 
 
• The SMR initiative aligns with the **Make in India** strategy, focusing on indigenous development of advanced technologies. 
 
• This will boost local industries, create jobs, and reduce dependency on foreign technology. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Budget Allocation:** The allocation of **Rs. 20,000 crores** reflects the Indian government’s commitment to advancing nuclear energy technologies. 
 
• **Energy Security:** SMRs will enhance India’s energy security by providing sustainable and reliable power for industrial and residential needs. 
 
• **Carbon Emission Reduction:** Nuclear energy is a clean energy source, and SMRs will play a significant role in reducing India’s dependence on fossil fuels and achieving **climate goals**. 
 
• **Global Collaboration:** India may collaborate with countries already leading in SMR development to gain technical expertise and accelerate deployment.

questions.question: Ashwini Bhide Deshpande is a renowned vocalist associated with which Gharana?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jaipur-Atrauli Gharana**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Ashwini Bhide Deshpande** is a renowned Hindustani classical vocalist belonging to the **Jaipur-Atrauli Gharana**. 

• The **Jaipur-Atrauli Gharana** is one of the prominent gharanas (musical lineages) of Hindustani classical music, known for its intricate raga development and a systematic approach to compositions. 

• She has been trained under the guidance of her mother, Manik Bhide, and has further honed her skills in the Jaipur-Atrauli style under the tutelage of Pandit Narayanrao Datar and Pandit Ratnakar Pai. 

• The hallmark of the Jaipur-Atrauli Gharana is its **unique repertoire of complex ragas**, including rare ragas and unconventional combinations. 

• Ashwini Bhide Deshpande is particularly celebrated for her mastery of such rare ragas and her ability to combine technical precision with emotional depth in her performances. 

• Her contributions to Hindustani classical music have earned her numerous accolades and recognition globally. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Jaipur-Atrauli Gharana:** 
 

• The gharana was founded by **Alladiya Khan** in the late 19th century and is named after the cities of Jaipur and Atrauli where the gharana flourished. 

• It is known for its **focus on melodic structure**, with a preference for intricate and slow elaboration of ragas. 

• The gharana emphasizes **rare and complex ragas**, such as Basanti Kedar, Sampoorna Malkauns, and others, which are seldom heard in other gharanas. 

• Its compositions often feature **layakari (rhythmic play)** and intricate taans (fast-paced melodic patterns). 

• Key exponents of this gharana include **Kesarbai Kerkar, Mogubai Kurdikar, Kishori Amonkar**, and now Ashwini Bhide Deshpande. 
 
 

• **Other Prominent Gharanas:** 
 

• **Banaras Gharana:** Known for its thumri and semi-classical styles, this gharana focuses on expressive and emotive renditions. 

• **Patiala Gharana:** Famous for its bold and intricate taans, this gharana is associated with artists like Bade Ghulam Ali Khan. 

• **Kirana Gharana:** Known for its emphasis on melody and note perfection, this gharana is associated with artists like Bhimsen Joshi and Abdul Karim Khan. 
 
 

• **Hindustani Classical Music:** 
 

• This is one of the two main traditions of Indian classical music, the other being Carnatic music. 

• It originated in North India and is deeply rooted in Vedic traditions and ancient musical texts like the Natya Shastra. 

• It is based on the concept of **ragas** (melodic frameworks) and **talas** (rhythmic cycles). 

• Renowned exponents include Ravi Shankar, Zakir Hussain, and Kishori Amonkar. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Gharana System:** 
 

• The gharana system is a lineage-based approach to teaching and performing Indian classical music. 

• Each gharana has its distinct style and repertoire, passed down from teacher to student. 

• It serves as a way to preserve and continue the rich traditions of Indian classical music. 
 
 

• **Ashwini Bhide Deshpande's Contributions:** 
 

• She has authored books on music and written compositions in various ragas. 

• Her performances emphasize both traditional purity and contemporary relevance.

questions.question: Who is the author of the book 'In an Antique Land'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Amitav Ghosh**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Amitav Ghosh** is the author of the book "**In an Antique Land**," which was published in **1992**. 

• The book is a blend of **historical narrative** and **ethnographic study**, combining the genres of fiction and non-fiction. 

• "In an Antique Land" explores themes such as **cultural exchanges**, **history**, **identity**, and **migration**. 

• It is set against the backdrop of **Egypt** and **India**, focusing on the **medieval trade network** between these two regions. 

• Amitav Ghosh is an acclaimed author of several other novels, including "**The Shadow Lines**" and "**The Glass Palace**," which also delve into themes of history and identity. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 

• **Amitav Ghosh:** 
 

• Amitav Ghosh was born on **11 July 1956** in **Calcutta, India**. 

• He is a recipient of several prestigious awards, including the **Padma Shri** in **2007** and the **Jnanpith Award** in **2018**. 

• Ghosh is renowned for his ability to weave **historical events** into compelling narratives, making him one of the leading authors in the genre of historical fiction. 
 
 

• **In an Antique Land:** 
 

• The book is a mix of historical research and personal narrative, offering a unique perspective on **cross-cultural connections**. 

• It is based on the author’s doctoral research at **Oxford University** and focuses on a 12th-century Jewish merchant and his Indian slave. 

• The book draws on the **Cairo Geniza** manuscripts, a treasure trove of historical documents preserved in Cairo's Ben Ezra Synagogue. 
 
 

• **Other Works by Amitav Ghosh:** 
 

• **The Circle of Reason (1986):** Ghosh’s debut novel, which won the **Prix Médicis étranger**. 

• **The Shadow Lines (1988):** A novel exploring the **partition of India** and its impact on families. 

• **The Ibis Trilogy:** A historical fiction series including "**Sea of Poppies**" (2008), "**River of Smoke**" (2011), and "**Flood of Fire**" (2015), centered around the **Opium Wars**. 
 
 

• **Neel Mukherjee:** 
 

• Author of novels like "**The Lives of Others**" (2014), which was shortlisted for the **Man Booker Prize**. 

• His works primarily delve into **family dynamics** and **social issues**. 
 
 

• **Manu Joseph:** 
 

• Known for his novel "**Serious Men**" (2010), which won the **PEN/Open Book Award**. 

• He frequently writes about **Indian society** and **politics**. 
 
 

• **Siddharth Dhanvant Shanghvi:** 
 

• Author of "**The Last Song of Dusk**" (2004), which won multiple awards, including the **Betty Trask Award**. 

• His works often explore themes like **love**, **loss**, and **identity**.

questions.question: Which of the following folk dance of Chhattisgarh is also known as 'Parrot dance'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Suwa Dance**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Suwa Dance** is a traditional folk dance of **Chhattisgarh**, primarily performed by women during the **Diwali festival.** 

• It is popularly known as the "**Parrot Dance**" because the dancers hold clay parrots in their hands while performing. 

• Suwa Dance is a **symbol of happiness** and is closely associated with the rural and tribal communities of Chhattisgarh. 

• This dance celebrates **nature, joy, and harvest**, showcasing gratitude towards the environment and expressing festivity. 

• The performers form a circle, singing songs and dancing rhythmically to the beats of traditional musical instruments like **dholak** and **mandar.** 

• The dance is deeply rooted in the **culture and traditions** of Chhattisgarh, demonstrating the artistic expressions of the tribal groups. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Kolatam Dance:** 
 

• It is a traditional folk dance from **Andhra Pradesh.** 

• Kolatam involves rhythmic stick movements and group formations, often performed during festivals. 

• It is a **social and devotional** dance form, reflecting the cultural heritage of Andhra Pradesh. 
 
 

• **Lambadi Dance:** 
 

• Lambadi is a folk dance of **Telangana** and **Andhra Pradesh**, primarily performed by the **Banjaras** or tribal communities. 

• It showcases vibrant costumes with mirrors and beads, and performers sing songs about daily life, nature, and festivities. 

• This dance form reflects the **nomadic lifestyle** of the Banjaras. 
 
 

• **Aoling Monyu Dance:** 
 

• Aoling Monyu is a traditional dance of the **Konyak tribe** in **Nagaland.** 

• It is performed during the **Aoling festival**, which marks the arrival of spring and the beginning of the new year. 

• The dance is accompanied by chants and songs, showcasing **tribal rituals** and celebrations of the harvest season. 
 
 

• **Chhattisgarh Folk Dances:** 
 

• Besides Suwa Dance, other notable folk dances of Chhattisgarh include **Panthi Dance**, **Raut Nacha**, and **Karma Dance**. 

• These dances are integral to the **tribal culture** and showcase the traditions, festivals, and lifestyle of the region. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Tribal Communities:** 
 

• Chhattisgarh is known for its **rich tribal heritage**, with a significant population of **Gonds, Baigas, and Oraons**. 

• Folk dances like Suwa Dance highlight the **cultural expressions** of these communities. 
 
 

• **Festivals of Chhattisgarh:** 
 

• Major festivals include **Diwali, Navakhai, and Bastar Dussehra**, which feature traditional dances and rituals. 

• These festivals reflect the **socio-religious** significance and vibrant culture of the state. 
 
 

• **Significance of Folk Dances:** 
 

• Folk dances are a medium to preserve **cultural identity**, traditions, and heritage. 

• They often involve storytelling, connecting the performers to their **roots and environment.**

questions.question: In the context of space research in India, what does "N" stands for in INCOSPAR? ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**National**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **INCOSPAR** stands for **Indian National Committee for Space Research**. The term "National" highlights the scope of the organization being centered on India's space research initiatives.

• **INCOSPAR** was established in **1962** under the leadership of Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, the father of the Indian space program.

• The inclusion of "National" signifies the committee's role in coordinating space research activities at a national level, ensuring development and collaboration across various scientific and technological domains within India.

• INCOSPAR later evolved into the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**, which is now India's premier space agency responsible for all space exploration and satellite programs.

• **Evolution of India's Space Program:**

• ISRO's achievements include the development of the **Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV)** and the **Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding Sale of government assets like sale of shares in Public sector unit (PSU)?

options.text: It creates liability for the government
Amount comes from sale of shares are part of capital receipts
Amount comes from sale of shares are part of revenue receipts
It does not reduce the total assets of the government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2: Amount comes from the sale of shares are part of capital receipts.**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 

__ 
 
• **Sale of government assets like PSU shares** is categorized under **capital receipts** because it involves the realization of capital assets, such as equity, by the government. 
 
• The funds raised through the sale of shares in Public Sector Units (PSUs) are **non-recurring in nature** and do not constitute a regular source of income for the government. 
 
• The amount received from such sales is used to **reduce the fiscal deficit or fund developmental activities**, rather than being treated as revenue receipts. 
 
• **Revenue receipts** include recurring income such as taxes and duties, whereas proceeds from disinvestment represent a **capital inflow**. 
 
• The sale of government shares in PSUs does not create liability for the government; instead, it reduces its ownership in these entities while generating funds. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Capital Receipts:** 
 
 
• Capital receipts are those receipts that **result in either an increase in liabilities or a reduction in assets** of the government. 
 
• Examples include **loans raised by the government**, disinvestment proceeds, borrowings from external sources, and recovery of loans. 
 
• They are used to **finance capital expenditure** or manage fiscal deficits. 
 
 
 
• **Revenue Receipts:** 
 
 
• Revenue receipts are government receipts that **do not create liabilities or reduce assets**. 
 
• They consist of **tax revenues (income tax, GST, etc.) and non-tax revenues** (interest, dividends, and fees). 
 
• These are used to meet the recurring expenses of the government, such as salaries, subsidies, and maintenance costs. 
 
 
 
• **Disinvestment:** 
 
 
• Disinvestment refers to the **sale or liquidation of government-owned assets or shares in PSUs**. 
 
• The primary objectives of disinvestment are **to reduce the fiscal burden, improve public finances, and enhance operational efficiency** in PSUs. 
 
• For example, the government’s disinvestment in companies like Air India and BPCL has been part of its fiscal strategy. 
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:** 
 
 
• Fiscal deficit is the difference between the government’s total expenditure and total revenue (excluding borrowings). 
 
• Proceeds from disinvestment are often utilized to **bridge the fiscal deficit** and reduce the government’s reliance on borrowing. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Statement 1:** "It creates liability for the government" is **incorrect**. The sale of assets does not create liability; instead, it reduces ownership in PSUs. 
 
• **Statement 2:** "Amount comes from the sale of shares are part of capital receipts" is **correct**. Such inflows are capital receipts as they affect the capital structure of the government. 
 
• **Statement 3:** "Amount comes from the sale of shares are part of revenue receipts" is **incorrect**. Revenue receipts involve recurring income, unlike disinvestment proceeds. 
 
• **Statement 4:** "It does not reduce the total assets of the government" is **incorrect**. The sale of shares reduces the government’s shareholding, thereby reducing its assets.

questions.question: Following the Industrial Policy _______ of India the government has set up a special board known as Foreign Investment Promotion Board.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1991**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **Industrial Policy of 1991** marked a significant economic reform in India aimed at liberalizing the Indian economy and integrating it into the global market. 

• This policy introduced measures such as **abolition of industrial licensing** for most industries, reducing the role of the public sector, and encouraging private investment. 

• To boost **foreign direct investment (FDI)**, the government established the **Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB)**. The FIPB was a special body created to facilitate and attract foreign investments into India. 

• The **primary function of FIPB** was to evaluate and approve proposals for FDI that did not fall under the automatic route and required government approval. 

• The **Industrial Policy of 1991** played a pivotal role in transforming India's economy from a protectionist model to a more market-oriented and globally connected economy. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Industrial Policy of 1991:** 
 

• The policy was introduced by the then Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh** under the leadership of Prime Minister **P. V. Narasimha Rao**. 

• It aimed to reduce the **bureaucratic control** over industries and boost private sector participation in industrial development. 

• The policy also emphasized **globalization**, **privatization**, and **liberalization** to enhance India's economic growth. 

• It allowed **foreign equity participation** up to a certain percentage in various sectors and permitted **FDI** in key industries. 
 
 

• **Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB):** 
 

• The FIPB was established under the **Ministry of Finance** to promote foreign investments in India. 

• It acted as a **single-window clearance system** for FDI proposals requiring approval. 

• The FIPB was abolished in **2017** as part of the government's effort to simplify the FDI process, and its functions were transferred to **concerned ministries and departments**. 
 
 

• **Features of Industrial Policy 1991:** 
 

• **Delicensing:** Most industries were exempted from licensing except for a few sectors like defense and hazardous chemicals. 

• **Disinvestment:** It reduced the role of the public sector by allowing privatization of public enterprises. 

• **Trade Liberalization:** The policy removed restrictions on imports and exports, making the Indian economy more open to global markets. 

• **Technology Transfer:** It encouraged the adoption of advanced technologies and collaboration with foreign firms. 
 
 

• **Impact of 1991 Reforms:** 
 

• The policy led to a **higher GDP growth rate**, improved infrastructure, and increased employment opportunities. 

• It boosted **foreign exchange reserves** and reduced India's dependency on external borrowings. 

• The **private sector** emerged as a key player in driving economic growth and innovation. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Historical Context:** Prior to 1991, the Indian economy operated under a **protectionist regime** characterized by heavy state control and limited private sector involvement. 

• The **economic crisis of 1991**, marked by **low foreign exchange reserves** and a **balance of payments deficit**, necessitated these reforms. 

• The **World Bank** and **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** provided financial assistance on the condition that India would liberalize its economy. 

• The 1991 policy reforms became a **turning point** in India's economic history, paving the way for sustained economic growth and development.

questions.question: In 2001-02, excise duty structure was rationalized to a single rate of _________ per cent CENVAT (Central Value Add Tax).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**16 per cent CENVAT**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 
__ 

• The **excise duty structure** was rationalized in the **financial year 2001-02** to a single rate of **16 per cent CENVAT**, simplifying the previous complex multi-rate system. 

• **CENVAT (Central Value Added Tax)** replaced the traditional excise duty structure to ensure uniform taxation and reduce cascading effects on goods and services. 

• This reform aimed to bring **transparency**, enhance **compliance**, and create a simplified taxation regime for manufacturers and producers in India. 

• The single rate of **16 per cent CENVAT** facilitated easier calculation and administration of excise duties, benefiting industries and reducing bureaucratic hurdles. 

• This rationalization was also part of the broader efforts to modernize India's taxation system and align it with global practices. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Excise Duty:** 
 

• Excise duty is a **tax levied on the manufacture of goods within the country**, and it is collected by the government from manufacturers or producers. 

• It is an **indirect tax**, meaning the burden is ultimately passed on to the consumer. 

• In India, excise duties are governed by the **Central Excise Act, 1944**. 
 
 

• **Objectives of CENVAT:** 
 

• **CENVAT** was introduced to **minimize the cascading effect** of taxes on products and services. 

• It promotes the concept of **value addition taxation**, where tax is applied only to the value added at each stage of production or distribution. 

• The system ensures **better input credit utilization**, allowing manufacturers to claim tax credits on inputs used for production. 
 
 

• **Reforms in Taxation:** 
 

• The rationalization of excise duty in 2001-02 was part of broader reforms to modernize India's taxation system. 

• Other significant reforms include the introduction of VAT (Value Added Tax) and later, the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** in 2017, which replaced multiple indirect taxes. 

• These reforms aimed to create a **unified and streamlined tax structure** for goods and services. 
 
 

• **Impact of Excise Duty Rationalization:** 
 

• The single rate of **16 per cent CENVAT** reduced administrative complexities for businesses. 

• It encouraged **compliance** and helped manufacturers focus on their operations rather than navigating complex tax structures. 

• It also improved **government revenue collection** by creating a more efficient taxation system. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Tax Credit:** 
 

• Under the **CENVAT Credit Rules**, manufacturers can claim tax credits for excise duties paid on inputs or raw materials used in production. 

• This system prevents the cascading effect of taxes and promotes efficiency in the taxation process. 
 
 

• **Predecessors to GST:** 
 

• Before the introduction of GST, taxes like **CENVAT**, VAT, and service tax formed the backbone of India's indirect taxation system. 

• GST consolidated these taxes into a single system, further simplifying the taxation process. 
 
 

• **Global Practices:** 
 

• The rationalization of excise duties aligns with international practices of simplifying indirect taxation. 

• Countries worldwide use VAT or similar systems to ensure efficient tax collection and minimize cascading effects. 
 
 
</ul

questions.question: The Contingency Fund of an Indian State is held by ________ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Governor**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **Contingency Fund of an Indian State** is established under **Article 267(2)** of the Constitution of India. It is maintained by each state to meet unforeseen expenditures. 

• The fund is placed at the disposal of the **Governor** of the state, who has the authority to make advances out of it to meet urgent and unforeseen expenditures pending authorization by the state legislature. 

• The fund is created by the state legislature through an act, specifying the total amount of the fund. This amount can vary from state to state. 

• The Governor can advance money from the Contingency Fund when immediate action is required, and there is no time to seek approval from the legislature. ***Hence, the correct option is Governor.*** 

• Once the expenditure is incurred, the state government must present it to the legislature for approval, and the amount withdrawn is subsequently recouped into the Contingency Fund. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Contingency Fund of India:** 
 

• At the Union level, the **Contingency Fund of India** is established under **Article 267(1)** of the Indian Constitution. It is at the disposal of the **President of India**. 

• It is used to meet unforeseen expenses that cannot wait for parliamentary approval. The fund is later replenished by the Parliament. 

• The corpus of the Contingency Fund of India is fixed at **Rs. 500 crore**, as prescribed by the Parliament. 
 
 

• **Difference between Consolidated Fund and Contingency Fund:** 
 

• The **Consolidated Fund** is the main account of the government where all revenues received, loans raised, and money received in repayment of loans are credited. Expenditures from this fund require legislative approval. 

• The **Contingency Fund**, on the other hand, is used for emergency expenditures that cannot wait for legislative approval. 
 
 

• **Role of the Governor in Finances:** 
 

• The Governor is the **constitutional head** of a state and has specific financial powers, including the authority to advance money from the Contingency Fund for urgent matters. 

• He/she acts on the advice of the state council of ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, in financial matters. 
 
 

• **Examples of Contingency Fund Usage:** 
 

• Natural disasters, such as floods, cyclones, or earthquakes, often require immediate financial assistance, which can be drawn from the Contingency Fund. 

• Emergency relief measures during pandemics or public health crises can also utilize this fund. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• The Contingency Fund is meant to ensure the smooth functioning of the government in times of financial emergencies. 

• It is a temporary arrangement, and all expenditures must later be approved by the legislature to maintain accountability and transparency. 

• Both the Union and the States in India have their respective Contingency Funds, managed by the President and Governors, respectively. 

• While the Governor has the authority to use the fund, the legislature plays a crucial role in ensuring proper checks and balances by approving or disapproving the expenditures.

questions.question: Which of the following port is confronted with the problem of silt accumulation in the Hugli River?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kolkata port**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kolkata Port**, officially known as the **Syama Prasad Mukherjee Port**, is located on the banks of the **Hugli River** in West Bengal, India.
 
• The port faces a major challenge due to **silt accumulation** in the Hugli River, which requires frequent dredging to maintain navigability.
 
• The problem of silt accumulation arises because the Hugli River is a distributary of the Ganges, carrying a heavy load of **sediment** deposited in the riverbed.
 
• This sedimentation significantly affects the port's **draft depth**, leading to difficulties in handling large vessels and increasing maintenance costs.
 
• The Kolkata Port relies on continuous dredging operations funded by the **Government of India** to ensure smooth functioning and to prevent disruptions in maritime trade.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kolkata Port:**

 
 
• Established in **1870**, it is one of the oldest operating ports in India.
 
• It serves as a crucial trade hub for the eastern and northeastern regions of India.
 
• It has two dock systems: **Kolkata Dock System** (KDS) and **Haldia Dock Complex** (HDC).
 
• The port primarily handles cargo such as **petroleum products, iron ore, fertilizers, and containers**.
 
 
 
• **Silt Accumulation in Hugli River:**
 
 
• The Hugli River is a tidal river, and its sediment load is influenced by the **monsoon season** and tides.
 
• Silt accumulation reduces the **draft depth**, making it challenging for large vessels to navigate.
 
• To combat this, the port authority conducts dredging operations to maintain a minimum draft level of **7 meters**.
 
• This issue is exacerbated by the river's complex **meandering patterns** and the presence of shifting sandbanks.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Ports:**
 
 
• **Kochchi Port:** Located in Kerala, it is a major port on the Arabian Sea and does not face issues of silt accumulation due to its coastal location.
 
• **Tuticorin Port:** Situated in Tamil Nadu, it is a deep-sea port handling large cargo vessels without challenges related to riverine siltation.
 
• **Chennai Port:** Also in Tamil Nadu, it is a coastal port with a natural harbor; it does not require extensive dredging compared to Kolkata Port.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• Silt accumulation increases operational costs due to regular dredging activities, impacting the port's profitability.
 
• It limits the port's ability to handle large vessels, affecting trade efficiency and capacity.
 
• The Government of India allocates significant funds annually to maintain navigability and ensure uninterrupted trade operations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hugli River Facts:**

 
 
• The Hugli River is a distributary of the **Ganges River**, flowing through West Bengal.
 
• Its sedimentation is influenced by **seasonal tides** and upstream erosion.
 
• The river is vital for inland trade but poses challenges for maritime navigation due to **sandbank formations**.
 
 
 
• **Dredging Technology:**
 
 
• Dredging involves removing **sediment deposits** to deepen waterways and maintain navigability.
 
• Advanced dredging equipment, such as **trailing suction hopper dredgers**, is employed at Kolkata Port.
 
• Continuous dredging ensures the port remains operational despite the natural sedimentation process.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• Kolkata Port played a crucial role in India's **colonial trade** as the gateway to the Bengal region.
 
• Post-independence, the port has remained a vital hub for **exports and imports** in eastern India.

questions.question: What was the primary function of Planning Commission of India?

options.text: To formulate and implement five year plans.
To monitor the currency exchange system in India.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To formulate and implement five-year plans.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Planning Commission of India** was established in **1950** by a resolution of the Government of India, under the chairmanship of the then Prime Minister **Jawaharlal Nehru**. Its primary objective was to formulate and implement **five-year plans** for the country’s socio-economic development.
 
• The Commission was tasked with assessing the resources of the country and devising strategies to utilize them efficiently for economic growth and development. **Hence, its primary function was to formulate and implement five-year plans.**
 
• The first **Five-Year Plan (1951-56)** focused on the agricultural sector to address food shortages and ensure self-sufficiency. Subsequent plans targeted various sectors like industrialization, poverty alleviation, and infrastructure.
 
• The Planning Commission coordinated between **central and state governments** to ensure the successful implementation of plans and programs, while also monitoring their progress and effectiveness.
 
• It also played a role in allocating resources across different sectors and regions, ensuring balanced development across the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Background:**
 
 
• The idea of central planning in India was inspired by the **Soviet Union**, where planning was used as a tool to achieve rapid industrialization and economic development.
 
• The Planning Commission was established on **15 March 1950**, following India's independence in 1947, to fulfill the vision of a planned economy.
 
 
 
• **Features of Five-Year Plans:**
 
 
• The Five-Year Plans were aimed at achieving specific objectives like **economic growth**, poverty reduction, employment generation, and regional balance.
 
• Each plan was based on detailed studies of national priorities and resource availability, ensuring comprehensive coverage of various sectors.
 
• The Planning Commission used a mix of **market mechanisms** and government intervention to achieve developmental goals.
 
 
 
• **Replacement of Planning Commission:**
 
 
• In 2015, the Planning Commission was replaced by the **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India) to align planning with the needs of a dynamic economy.
 
• NITI Aayog focuses on **policy formulation, cooperative federalism, and real-time monitoring** of developmental progress instead of fixed five-year plans.
 
 
 
• **Functions of NITI Aayog:**
 
 
• Unlike the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog acts as a think-tank and provides **policy advice** to both central and state governments.
 
• It emphasizes **bottom-up planning** and involves states as equal partners in the development process.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1:** "To control the inflation" is incorrect because the Planning Commission was not directly responsible for inflation control. This function falls under the purview of monetary and fiscal policies managed by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and the Ministry of Finance.
 
• **Option 2:** "To boost the foreign trade" is incorrect as foreign trade policies were managed by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not the Planning Commission.
 
• **Option 4:** "To monitor the currency exchange system in India" is incorrect because this responsibility lies with the **Reserve Bank of India** and not the Planning Commission.
 
• The Planning Commission's focus was on long-term development strategies, resource allocation, and sectoral planning, which makes **Option 3 the correct answer.**

questions.question:
Which of the following statement is correct regarding haemoglobin in humans?

I. In humans it is the respiratory pigment

II. It has very low affinity for oxygen
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
 
 
• **Statement I:** In humans, **haemoglobin serves as the respiratory pigment**. It is primarily responsible for the transport of oxygen from the lungs to tissues and organs and the return of carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs for exhalation. *Hence, this statement is correct.* 
 
• **Statement II:** The claim that haemoglobin has a very low affinity for oxygen is incorrect. In fact, haemoglobin has a **high affinity for oxygen**, which allows it to efficiently bind oxygen in the lungs and release it in tissues where oxygen is required. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
 
• Haemoglobin is a protein found in red blood cells that contains iron. The iron component plays a vital role in binding oxygen molecules. 
 
• Oxygen binds to haemoglobin in the lungs, forming oxyhaemoglobin, and is then transported to various parts of the body. 
 
• Haemoglobin also assists in the transport of carbon dioxide back to the lungs, where it is expelled during respiration.

questions.question: The summaries of conferences held in ancient India were called _______ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Samhitas**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
 
 
• **Samhitas** are the earliest and most fundamental texts of the **Vedic literature**, forming the core of ancient Indian knowledge systems. 
 
• They contain **hymns, prayers, and rituals** dedicated to various deities, as well as philosophical thoughts and cosmological concepts. 
 
• The **Samhitas** are divided based on the respective Vedic branch they belong to: **Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda.** 
 
• These texts were compiled to preserve the oral traditions and were used during **ancient Indian conferences and discussions** as references for rituals, spiritual practices
